newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bonds end stronger, bills still chained to kiwi.
newsitem.headline: NZ bonds end stronger, bills still chained to kiwi.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close

* NZ bonds hold gains after morning rally, buoyed by US mkt
* Bill rates end touch lower, still chained to currency
* Long end seen less influenced by volatile short end
New Zealand's key 90-day bank bill rate closed a shade lower on Wednesday after being pushed around in a wide range by the volatile Kiwi dollar.
Dealers said the short end was still chained to the currency and would continue to track its movements.
"It was a little bit hectic this morning. We must have traded about a 8.49-68 (percent) range in the 90-days," said one dealer. "We rallied down to about 49 and then just sold back."
The Kiwi bounced above 65 U.S. cents at the open from its overnight low of 0.6455, prompting a good rally in the short end, but then gave up its gains and forced rates higher again.
"The Kiwi rules the bill market at the moment," the dealer said.
By the close, the Kiwi had recovered somewhat to 0.6490/97 and 64.40 on its Trade-Weighted Index.
Bonds rallied strongly in early trade, buoyed by solid offshore buying and U.S. Treasury strength overnight, and held their gains in afternoon trade when Australia also rallied.
"There was some good buying last night and even if the Kiwi had come down to 0.6450 I suspect there still would have been bids around in the long end," said a senior bond dealer.
He said Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony had injected "a very positive sentiment right through the global market".
U.S. Treasuries rallied strongly when Greenspan told Congress the U.S. economy's growth was slowing for now and inflation in 1997 would be modest.

"The Aussie market's been pretty good today and obviously the U.S. market was on fire last night. I think you'll see a continuation of that move tonight, so we could easily see lower long bond yields again tomorrow," the dealer said, adding that the long end was divorcing itself from the short end somewhat.
"That's what we've seen today, the long end has traded pretty much independently of the shorts, and I think that's going to continue."
